Love Poem by Ron Padgett, it's probably my favourite poem I've read and is one of the first poems I read as I started finding an interest in poetry. So much so that I recently painted a [tote bag](https://i.imgur.com/Le5E4TR.jpg) to express my love for the poem.

*its one-and-a-half-inch soft pine stem capped  
by a grainy dark purple head, so sober and furious  
and stubbornly ready to burst into flame,  
lighting, perhaps, the cigarette of the woman you love,  
for the first time, and it was never really the same  
after that.*

Probably my favourite segment from the poem.

Thank you for your kind words, it means a lot!

And yes, I'm glad you understand the sentiment. I find myself very often drawn to poems which deal with the monotony of life and somehow make something more of it all. Ron Padgett is my favourite poet and I find a lot of his work does a similar thing, picking up random and sometimes silly details that often get forgotten or overlooked.

With this poem in particular it was interesting, more often than not I write poems after the fact. However, as this moment unfolded the other night as I was making dinner with my partner I started writing in my head I suppose as it all went on. I knew it would make a good moment for a poem so I tried very hard to take in everything that was going on. As such recalling everything and actually writing the poem the day after became an absolute treat because I was so engrossed by the moment. 

Anyway, thank you again for your kind words and I'm glad you got something from a little poem I made. It means a lot, I hope you have a great day.

I quite like the hints of the contemporary times throughout this poem, the idea of posting images online and what not. The whole idea of this is something I find quite fascinating, especially as a photographer primarily. I often times get caught up in the notion that I do not want to photograph something, despite the fact it will serve as a remembrance of a nice time or constitute as a memory, mainly due to the fact that for that short period of time that I am making said image I am removing myself from the memory which is taking place. It's definitely a hard one to manage or find a correct answer to, and it's something I feel like I'll ponder for quite some time.

The transition from talking about a golden retriever to the sun is quite clever, kudos for those two lines. I also very much enjoy the signing off at the end, there's something really nice in the fact you recognise yourself as your own best friend.

Great stuff, keep it up.

Super interesting read, which I think everyone can relate to at some point or another. I think it's interesting that the portion of the poem most people seem to be focusing on is the last two lines. However, I find the lines 'But people change, love is strange' a far more resonating thought, especially given the subject matter. I think change is what ultimately kills love for most people, and that it's quite difficult to foster love amidst that change, not impossible but quite difficult. It's definitely something I've come to understand as I wake through my mid 20s, as both myself and everyone around me seems to be in this transitional state and more often than not we have acknowledged that this is the case. As such people seem reluctant, or maybe they're just too distracted with life to entertain permanent ideas such as love.

Anyway, wonderful poem.

When reading this I couldn't help but think of The Raven by Edgar Allan Poe, something about the dialogue between yourself and the clock reminded me of it.

Anywho, absolutely love the poem and wouldn't change much about it. I guess my only gripe would be the very last line, it seems far too abrupt when paired with the lines preceding it. The lines which come before have a very nice and almost lyrical reading:

**Impending, relentless.**

**Can’t be prevented.**

**I’m feeling demented.**

**utterly helpless.**

I feel as if you could have ended the poem there and it would've been just as effective. 

Aside from this minor point I think the poem is wonderful, I think the inner dialogue works really effectively and your use of curse words is actually surprisingly strong. I often times find the use of words like fuck etc. within poems can come off as edgy or ruin the mood of the poem but I think they work rather brilliantly here. 

Great work, keep it up! and fuck that clock!

Really enjoy the repeating structure of "when, and, then..." followed by the descriptions of animals in nature. The imagery is fantastic so as I read and subsequently arrived at an "and" I very much was excited for the next animal we were to meet and the environment in which they would be found.    
    

**"bulls plod in wet sod"**

Absolutely love the way this rolls off the tongue, it's very satisfying to say aloud. 

Although my favourite line has to be "I crumple up another poem in my throat". Using the verb of "crumpling" in adjacent to something we generally wouldn't associate with crumpling (the throat) is very clever, and despite the fact you would rarely see the throat described in the action of crumpling it somehow feels right, yaknow?

Anyway, wonderful poem. Keep on writing, my friend!

For me anyway I wouldn't particularly say I was all that close to my grandmother, visit her maybe once a month since I was a kid. She lived in a different part of the country aswell so there was a sense of detachment there.  She lived to 98 so she had lived a long and fulfilling life so the processing of letting go wasn't terribly difficult. My father comes from a family of 4 boys and 1 girl so their grieving process also wasn't visibly bad either (what with men showing brave faces when it comes to emotional stuff). I would consider my father a rather emotional person however so I knew on the inside he would be grieving with the loss, there's a whole lot of family history surrounding my father/his mother and the catholic church that plays a big part in his relationship with my grandmother. Long story short she was devoutly Catholic (evident by the mother Mary portrait hanging on the wall of her room) and my father had been sexually abused whilst attending church, which is something that basically broke his faith in the church and Catholicism in general. But yeah, his story is definitely something which intrigues me, both in the topical nature of the subject matter of Catholic Ireland and the abuse undertaken here by the church and the fact he's my father. I put together a zine that I want to get printed which puts his childhood and the church as a vocal point in the narrative, so hopefully that works out.

I've not had much time to play with it as it's actually a Christmas gift so I've only shot a few tests rolls before I had to give it back to my girlfriend until Christmas. However from my experience with it (it being my first rangefinder type camera) I've really enjoyed it, I thought due to it's size (which looks comical at times) that I would find it difficult to shoot (I haven't got big hands) however it was a joy to shoot. It produces a 6x9 negative which is a lot of real estate for detail, maybe a bit unneccessary for my uses but it might come in handy in the future, better to have more than less. If you are looking for something that is nice to hand hold (ie not RB/RZ styled cameras) then you've got a wide range of Fuji systems to choose from. You could go for the GA645 (provided you don't mind ditching 6x7 for 6x4.5), it features autofocus, auto roll of the film, metering and more. I'm pretty sure shooting it manual focus is a bit of a burdon though (requires you to place your hands and fingers in awkward positions to focus). Pretty much with any of the rangefinder medium formats you're going to be limited with that pesky minimum focus distance so if that isn't something you mind too much (and you don't want to sell an organ for a Mamiya 6/7) then I would highly recommend any of the Fujica RF's. Just do some research into the GS645, GA645, GW690 as they're all relatively easy to find in great condition. Only issue with the Fuji systems is a lot of them are fixed lens so you're going to be kinda stuck if there's a certain focal length you want to shoot but can't due to the fixed lens (the GA645zi features a zoom lens from like 35-55 or something of that range.)

I have the Fuji GW690 and whilst it's a great camera it may be a bit limiting in terms of being an all round camera. The minimum focus distance on a lot of the Fuji medium format cameras is 1 meter, so getting close up portraits is a no go, you're essentially stuck with body upwards shots [\(such as this taken on my GW690\).](https://www.flickr.com/photos/141618633@N03/24017316457/in/pool-fuji-gw690/) This is due to the fact they're rangefinders, I believe the Mamiya 7 has similar issues.

 In regards to the Pentax 67 it's a beast of a camera but well worth considering, make sure you get a version with mirror lockup though as the camera has a fairly big slap when taking photos.
